pages.x: The Atacama, on the Pacific coast of South America, is the driest desert on earth, but it held nitrate, prized for fertiliser and explosives. Chilean companies mined it on Bolivian land. When Bolivia raised a tax on one of them and moved to seize its property, Chilean troops took the port of Antofagasta, on 14 February 1879.

Peru had a secret alliance with Bolivia, so Chile declared war on both. The war began at sea. At Iquique, on 21 May, the Peruvian ironclad Huáscar rammed and sank the old wooden Esmeralda. Her captain, Arturo Prat, leapt onto the enemy's deck with his sword and was shot down. Chile made him its greatest hero.

For months the Huáscar's captain, Miguel Grau, raided the Chilean coast, and won his enemies' respect by rescuing the Esmeralda's survivors and writing to Prat's widow. On 8 October 1879 the Chilean fleet trapped the Huáscar off Angamos, and Grau was killed. With the sea lost, Peru's coast lay open.

Chile landed an army in the desert in November 1879 and took the nitrate province of Tarapacá. In May 1880 it routed the Peruvian and Bolivian armies at Tacna, and Bolivia all but left the war. On 7 June Chilean infantry stormed the Morro, the great rock fortress above Arica, in less than an hour.

In January 1881 a Chilean army of about 26,000 men broke the defences of Lima at Chorrillos and Miraflores, and marched into the Peruvian capital. The seaside town of Chorrillos was burned and looted. Chile occupied Lima for almost three years, and carried off thousands of books from the national library.

Peru fought on from the mountains. General Andrés Avelino Cáceres led soldiers and highland villagers in a guerrilla war against the occupation, and in July 1882 his men wiped out a Chilean garrison at Concepción. But Chile beat him at Huamachuco in 1883, and Peru made peace.

By the Treaty of Ancón in 1883 Peru gave up Tarapacá, and Chile kept Tacna and Arica; Tacna was handed back in 1929. Bolivia signed a truce in 1884, and in 1904 a treaty that gave up its whole coast. It has been landlocked ever since.

The nitrate fields made Chile rich for half a century, and the strongest power on the Pacific coast of South America. Bolivia has never accepted the loss of its sea: it keeps a navy on Lake Titicaca, marks a Day of the Sea every March, and took Chile to the world court, which ruled against it in 2018.

Chile won the sea and took Lima
